subject: physics
title: Potentials and Equipotentials
welcome_lead: Climb a potential well, traverse an equipotential — energy per unit charge or mass.
meta_desc: A-Level Fields adventure on electric and gravitational potential and equipotential surfaces.
final_note: Field lines and equipotentials always meet at right angles.

walkthroughs.body_html: V = Q / (4π ε₀ r). Positive charge gives positive potential, decreasing with r. Work done moving charge q from infinity to r is W = qV.
V = -GM/r. Gravity is always attractive, so V is taken as zero at infinity and negative everywhere else. Work to escape: -mV at surface.
Moving along an equipotential surface requires no work because ΔV = 0. Equipotentials are perpendicular to field lines everywhere.

mcqs.q: Work done moving charge q through ΔV is:
In which direction does an electric field point near a positive charge?
options: Radially inwards because positive attracts negative.
There is no field around a positive charge unless another charge is present.
It doubles — more distance means more space for gravity to act through.
Radially outwards — the field is defined by the force on a positive test charge, which is repelled.

mcqs.q: What does gravitational field strength at a point represent?
options: The mass of the object creating the field.
The total gravitational force at that point regardless of mass.
The force per unit mass that would act on a test mass placed at that point.
There is no field around a positive charge unless another charge is present.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two masses doubles, what happens to the gravitational force between them?
options: It halves — gravitational force is inversely proportional to distance.
The mass of the object creating the field.
It doubles — more distance means more space for gravity to act through.
It quarters — gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
